name: Bianca Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, twenty-seven, and I lead three electricians on repairs and small building jobs. My two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence let me sign off difficult work, but our little firm pays poorly. I use AI every day to sort supplier lists and draft customer messages, then I spend most of the day with cables and a tester.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a good day, and what's hard outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Finding a hidden fault before anyone pulls a whole wall apart feels wonderful. I live alone above a bakery, and after rent I've got about three weeks of expenses saved. There aren't many other firms nearby, so being the clever one doesn't give me much bargaining power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew we can stop talking about miracle software and finish the houses already booked. A customer still wants the sockets safe before the plasterer arrives. Small tools are useful without becoming a whole religion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is the worry, even if AI goes quiet. My master electrician's licence doesn't give my rent a discount. With so few local employers, losing one week's work would mean asking my brother for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair shifts and ask the owner for a written pay review next month. Now and through the first year of this picture, I'd put twenty a week into a separate emergency account if every bill is covered. I won't borrow to buy a shiny new tester while the old one works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about money rather than machines. Getting paid late makes my stomach tighten before I even open the banking app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the pay request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd list the faults I've found, the callbacks avoided and the jobs I sign off. I believe you should earn a rise by showing the work, though I can't make the owner agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the twenty isn't available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The saving waits; rent doesn't. I'd ask my brother for a lift instead of paying for a taxi after a late call, but I haven't needed a cash loan yet.

say: I'd tell the crew to finish **booked houses** rather than argue about miracle software.
I think **small tools** can help without changing the whole trade.
think: My **low pay** worries me even when AI makes little difference to work.
I have **three weeks saved** and few nearby employers to bargain with.
do: Keep the **repair shifts** and request a written pay review next month.
Save **twenty weekly** only after covering bills during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about late pay and a short financial cushion.
S0.quote: My master electrician's licence doesn't give my rent a discount.
fieldNote: Her **qualification** and responsibility exceed what the small firm pays, leaving her exposed despite strong practical skills.
She frames a **pay rise** as earned value while admitting the owner can still refuse her request.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts while requesting a written pay review next month
Save twenty weekly when all bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the software chase delivery dates, but don't pretend an estimate repairs a burnt connection. I'd show the apprentice how I check its parts list against the actual board. A cheaper office shouldn't mean a careless site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on job should hold up, but fewer office hours could mean the owner tries to squeeze more visits into my day. If customers expect lower prices, our already small wage pot could get tighter. I don't know whether saved office time reaches us as money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd spend fifteen minutes each evening testing the AI parts lists against completed jobs, without customer details. In the first year I'd ask for a trial where I handle the new quoting tool during paid hours, with my repair shifts kept. If the owner refuses paid time, I won't do the firm's office job free at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested and still anxious. I like being quick with a new tool, but speed hasn't paid my rent any more reliably yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would make you stop the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong cable size is enough to stop using that result. I'd check the real load and the rules myself, not hand a customer a neat page and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want the extra responsibility but won't do it free. How would you explain that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain the limit clearly. My current wage buys a full working day already. The owner can choose a paid trial or keep doing the quotes; I can't afford to donate my evenings.

say: I'd use software for **delivery dates** while keeping electrical checks with the electrician.
I'd show the apprentice why a **parts list** needs checking against the real board.
think: My **hands-on work** should continue, but tighter visit targets could make the same wage harder to earn.
I don't know whether **office savings** will improve my pay or squeeze it further.
do: Test **AI parts lists** against completed jobs for fifteen minutes each evening.
Request a **paid quoting trial** with repair shifts retained during the first year.
feel: **Interested but anxious** about receiving extra work without extra pay.
S1.quote: My current wage buys a full working day already.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** makes experimentation familiar, but she draws a clear boundary around unpaid work for the employer.
She expects **physical repairs** to persist while recognising that pricing pressure can still reach her own earnings.

steps.text: Test AI parts lists against completed jobs for fifteen minutes nightly
Request a paid quoting trial while keeping repair shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is short enough that every small contractor needs an honest plan. Let firms compete, but tell apprentices when the work they are learning might change. I'd rather hear an awkward answer now than a cheerful surprise later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quoting and planning change in 2028; the difficult repairs still need hands until robots catch up around 2031. I expect a serious hit to my wages once contractors can buy those machines, though I can't tell how fast small firms will afford them. Three weeks of savings isn't enough to fund a brave speech about starting my own company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask two distant contractors about advertised service jobs that include paid training, applying only where the wage covers rent and travel. In the first year after 2028 I'd take a suitable offer only in writing, before leaving this job. I'd also set up a weekly call with my brother now to agree what temporary help he could actually offer if shifts disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, even though I can think of things to try. I lie awake imagining my tool bag by the door with nowhere paid to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your brother for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A spare room for a month if I lose the flat, not a promise to cover every bill. My brother has his own rent, so I'd ask what is real rather than assume family money exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look farther away before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The few firms here would all be chasing the same customers. I'd use the years when repairs still pay to reach a larger service team, but a job title alone doesn't guarantee safety after 2031.

say: I'd ask small contractors for an **honest plan** before two years disappear.
I'd want apprentices told how **their work** might change rather than given false comfort.
think: I expect a **serious wage hit** when capable robots reach contractors around 2031.
My **three-week cushion** cannot fund a business launch while I search for safer paid work.
do: Apply for **advertised service jobs** only where paid training, wages and travel costs fit.
Arrange a **weekly family call** to agree possible temporary housing if shifts disappear.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing income despite having conditional job applications to pursue.
S2.quote: Three weeks of savings isn't enough to fund a brave speech about starting my own company.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 planning** changes from later physical competition, without treating the interval as permanent protection for her wage.
Her **family support** request is limited and negotiated, while a move between employers requires an affordable written offer.

steps.text: Apply for advertised service jobs offering affordable wages and paid training
Agree possible one-month emergency housing with my brother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us room to negotiate paid learning while the repair work still comes in. Firms that train good electricians could keep good electricians. I don't want a certificate bought just to impress a customer online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I can build some money and test training without betting the rent. Planning changes in 2031 and robots follow around 2034, when I'll only be thirty-five. My income could still shrink, but I needn't make a rushed leap this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving thirty a week from November if the bills allow, and ask for a paid place on a practical equipment-servicing course next year. I'd enrol only if the employer pays the fee and keeps my wage during class. In the first year after 2031 I'd use the new planning tools on supervised repair jobs, checking whether the training still leads to paid tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I can breathe while I make the list. A longer warning changes how much I can do before I need an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer pays the fee but not your time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then that particular course waits. I can't trade a week's rent for a certificate, however keen I sound when I ask about new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving thirty mean in your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer evening takeaways after callouts, mainly. I'd cook at my brother's once a week and bring portions home, though a broken van or a rent increase could interrupt the saving.

say: I'd ask firms to provide **paid learning** while repair jobs still bring money in.
I want **practical training**, not a certificate bought for advertising.
think: Five years lets me **build money** and test training without risking this month's rent.
My **income could shrink** after planning changes in 2031 and robots follow around 2034.
do: Save **thirty weekly** from November when bills allow, reducing takeaway meals after callouts.
Enrol in **equipment servicing** only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages during class.
Use **new planning tools** on supervised repair jobs in the first year after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough breathing room to carry out a conditional plan.
S3.quote: I can't trade a week's rent for a certificate, however keen I sound when I ask about new machines.
fieldNote: Her **training plan** depends on both fees and wages being covered, rather than curiosity supplying money she does not have.
The **longer warning** reduces urgency without removing exposure to lower earnings while she is still early in her working life.

steps.text: Save thirty weekly when bills allow by buying fewer takeaways
Enrol in equipment servicing only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Check new planning tools on supervised repair jobs after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to keep working and prepare properly, provided we start. I'd favour apprenticeships that pay people while they learn the changing work. Families shouldn't have to guess which glossy course has real work behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be thirty-seven when thinking AI arrives in 2036, and forty when the robots follow around 2039. Neither is retirement age, but I could have years of different repair experience by then. My money is still thin now, so I won't describe this whole future as comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the saving plan from the five-year picture and ask next month to rotate onto commercial maintenance visits. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare real service vacancies and apply where wages cover my bills, rather than assume my experience buys a post. I would keep testing AI fault-note tools now, using invented examples rather than customer records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the present and more hopeful about the room to change. Ten years doesn't pay this winter's rent, but it gives me more winters to build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why commercial maintenance rather than buying robots yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn from the crew and earn while I do it. Buying a machine would need money I don't have, and I'd want actual prices and contracts before imagining ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as preparation going badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If two years passed and I still had three weeks saved, no new visits and only promises about training, I'd start applying farther afield. A long warning is only useful if I check what I did with it.

say: I'd support **paid apprenticeships** that teach changing work while people still earn.
I'd want families shown **real work** behind a course before paying for it.
think: I'll still need **earned income** at thirty-seven in 2036 and forty when robots follow around 2039.
My **thin savings now** keep me worried despite having more time to gain repair experience.
do: Continue **conditional saving** and ask next month for commercial maintenance visits.
Test **AI fault notes** using invented examples without customer information.
Apply for **real service vacancies** after 2036 only where wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious now**, but hopeful about having more time to gain experience and savings.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't pay this winter's rent, but it gives me more winters to build a cushion.
fieldNote: She does not mistake **a decade** of warning for retirement security, because she will still be forty when robots arrive.
Her **learning route** stays tied to paid visits and affordable vacancies instead of an unfunded plan to buy machines.

steps.text: Continue saving thirty weekly when household bills allow
Test AI fault notes using invented customer examples
Apply after 2036 for service vacancies whose wages cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my pay could be squeezed before I've built any spare money. Paid practical training with my wage kept would help more than a free evening lecture. I want a route from my present work to a job an employer is actually offering.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what skill pays, as well as what skill someone has. I can find a dangerous fault in a wall and still need my brother's sofa if the wages stop. Being good at work and being secure aren't the same thing.

headlineQuote: Being good at work and being secure aren't the same thing.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old lead electrician** with a technical diploma and master licence, but low pay leaves three weeks saved.
She uses **AI daily** and likes trying tools while refusing to give an employer unpaid evenings.
She expects **2028** to bring the sharpest pressure and considers distant vacancies only with affordable written offers.
Longer warnings support **conditional saving** and paid training, while present rent keeps her anxious even with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could squeeze her pay before she builds a financial cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** with maintained wages and a link to an actual vacancy would help.
